# Report: The Time Traveller's theory of Time

## 1. The question, frozen
The piece answers several questions. The one the title and opening make central: **what makes movement through Time possible, and can a machine do it?** Range: the dinner-table argument and the model demonstration. What is asked: forward — what *produces* travel through Time. (His later eight-day trip is a larger, different question, still being told when the excerpt stops.)

## 2. The explanation in parts
(a) Any real body extends in Length, Breadth, Thickness, **and Duration**.
(b) The distinction we draw between Time and the three Space dimensions is unreal; it comes only from our consciousness sliding along Time.
(c) We are always moving along Time, at a fixed rate, cradle to grave.
(d) We cannot stop or reverse because we lack the means — as a savage cannot rise six feet.
(e) A civilised man rose against gravitation in a balloon; so he might hope to slow, stop, or reverse his drift through Time.
(f) A machine with two levers travels indifferently in any direction of Space and Time.
(g) The model vanished on cue; the Psychologist explains it went too fast to see.

## 3. Part by part

| Part | Mark | Why |
|---|---|---|
| (a) four dimensions incl. Duration | **fixed** | The owner's stipulation. Not tested; "Duration" is set by definition, then used. |
| (b) the distinction is unreal | **held if** | Held only by the job "why is Time treated as different?" — a job the Medical Man supplies. Drop that job and the part does nothing. |
| (c) we always drift along Time | **held** | Held by the everyday fact that moments pass and we age (the barometer trace stands for it). But it answers "what can we tell from what we see", not "what produces motion". |
| (d) we can't stop or reverse | **held** | Held by the plain fact that nobody revisits a moment. |
| (e) balloon analogy | **loose** | Swap the balloon for the lift or the ship and it works as well. The shared, held thing is "difficulty is a matter of degree, not kind". The balloon itself is decoration. |
| (f) the two-lever machine | **fixed** | A design choice; either lever could be reversed and nothing breaks. |
| (g) "too fast to see" | **loose** | The patch that rescues the vanishing. It would swallow any invisibility. No gauge: nothing is named that would show it failing. |

Also: **the candle blowing out — idle.** Remove it; the model still vanishes. (The Medical Man "laid considerable stress" on it, but no job fails without it.) **The risk of stopping — asserted.** No poke is offered; never tested.

## 4. Whole-explanation checks
- **Flip.** Had the model stayed put, the levers "failed" and the theory stands. Had the candle flared instead of dying, the same. The theory covers the opposite of its own demonstration.
- **Reverse.** The invisibility story runs backwards from the result (it vanished) to a cause (too fast). Fine for "what can we tell"; not for "what produces".
- **Answer hidden in the starting points.** (a) puts "Time is a dimension we move along" in under the name "Duration"; (e) then recovers it as a licence to travel. The conclusion sits in the premise.
- **Where the jobs came from.** (a)–(d) given by the owner; "why is Time treated differently?" given by the Medical Man; "future or past?" *added* by the Psychologist and absorbed, not answered.
- **Pairs that pull.** (c) says we *do* move along Time; (d) says we *cannot* move about in Time. The pair is patched with "we can't control it". The line is now "we move but can't steer" — narrower than (b)'s "the distinction is unreal". What would show the line is misplaced: any case of steering.
- **Catch-all with no gauge.** "Presentation below the threshold" absorbs any unseeable result. Nothing is named that would show it swallowing a job.
- **What the change list leaves out.** How the candle died; whether the trip was to past or future — left out silently, not as a stated limit.
- **Best rival.** Sleight-of-hand. Nothing on the list tells the two apart: the machine vanishes either way. The narrator's confidence is testimony, not a change.
- **Where each part came from.** (b) **borrowed** from the popular "Fourth Dimension" talk of the day; (c)–(d) **built** from everyday facts; (e) **asserted** analogy; (g) **asserted**.

## 5. What would make it hardest to vary
One job. Send the model to a stated date and bring it back with something only that date could supply — a coin of a future reign. That single change separates time-travel from the trick and from "too fast to see". Without it the demonstration tests the trick, not the theory.

## 6. What this does not show
Hard to vary is not the same as true. The theory could be tight and wrong, or loose and right. This report sorts which parts are held in place; it does not decide whether time travel is possible.

## 7. One next step
Before the big machine runs, write down one prediction the model cannot make if it is only a trick — a dated object, or a second appearance on cue — and try that.
